summary.text: A 21-year-old male with a documented history of cannabis-induced psychosis, previously treated with depot paliperidone and non-compliant with follow-up and medication after discharge, was brought to the emergency department after three to four days of mutism, markedly reduced oral intake, insomnia and social withdrawal. His family reported ongoing cannabis use. One year earlier he had been hospitalized for acute psychosis that resolved with antipsychotic treatment, without catatonic features.

On arrival he was alert but minimally responsive with thought blocking, monotone speech and a perplexed affect. Examination showed psychomotor retardation, mild waxy flexibility, negativism and periods of decreased responsiveness, with blood pressure 154/93 mmHg and pulse 122 beats/minute. Creatine kinase was 25016 U/L with mildly increased creatinine, urine toxicology was positive for THC, and CT head and chest X-ray showed no acute abnormalities; ECG showed sinus tachycardia.

The diagnosis was cannabis-induced catatonia, with alternative causes excluded, complicated by rhabdomyolysis, early acute kidney injury and autonomic instability with recurrent tachycardia. He was admitted on one-to-one observation and given intravenous fluids and lorazepam; aripiprazole was introduced on day three and clonazepam added on day four, and tachycardia was monitored. Electroconvulsive therapy was not required.

The estimated BFCRS score was 22/69 on admission and about 15/69 within 48 hours, with increased responsiveness and improved oral intake. By day seven CK had normalised, renal function had improved and the estimated BFCRS was about 5/69; the patient became more conversational and compliant. Over the hospital stay catatonic features gradually improved, with residual mild psychomotor slowing and psychotic ideation.
